title: Ballet Star Tiler Peck to Make London West End Debut in Susan Stroman’s ‘Little Dancer’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: New York City Ballet principal dancer Tiler Peck will make her West End debut in “Little Dancer,” the Lynn Ahrens and Stephen Flaherty musical about
body:
New York City Ballet principal dancer Tiler Peck will make her West End debut in “Little Dancer,” the Lynn Ahrens and Stephen Flaherty musical about the girl who posed for Edgar Degas’ famous sculpture. 

	It opens at London’s Theatre Royal Haymarket on Feb. 15, 2027. Susan Stroman directs and choreographs the limited run, which will close on March 27. 

	The musical follows Marie van Goethem, a poor 14-year-old who wanted to become a great dancer and ended up as the model for Degas’ iconic sculpture. It’s set in Belle Époque Paris. The show previously sold out runs in Washington, D.C., and Seattle, as well as a 2025 concert performance at London’s Theatre Royal Drury Lane.
	

	Julian Ovenden (“High Society,” “Downton Abbey”) will play Degas. Laura Pitt-Pulford (“Standing at the Sky’s Edge,” “Seven Brides for Seven Brothers”) plays the adult Marie, and Josefina Gabrielle (“Chicago,” “Les Misérables”) plays Martine. All three have been Olivier nominees.


	“Many people know of the ‘Little Dancer’ sculpture, but few know much about the girl, the muse, who inspired it,” Peck said. “This show is about two determined artists willing to do anything for their craft, and it reveals a whole new side to Degas’ masterpiece.”

	Stroman has won five Tony Awards and two Oliviers, and her credits include “The Producers,” “Crazy for You,” “Contact” and “Oklahoma!” Ahrens, who writes the book and lyrics, and composer Flaherty are also Tony and Olivier winners. Their credits include “Ragtime,” “Anastasia” and “Once on This Island.”

	“Just as Degas was inspired by Marie, Marie inspired me,” Stroman said. “She wanted to be a great dancer, and inadvertently, through art, became the most famous dancer in the world.”
	

	Ovenden is going back to the Haymarket for the production. He said Ahrens and Flaherty had written “a deeply moving show about art, ambition and the lives of artists.” He added: “I also feel incredibly lucky to be surrounded by such extraordinary women at the very top of their game – Susan Stroman, Tiler Peck, Laura Pitt-Pulford and Josefina Gabrielle.”

	Peck was recently named NYCB’s first Choreographic Associate, the first woman to hold a choreographic title in the company’s history. She won an Emmy for the PBS “Great Performances” documentary “Tiler Peck: Suspending Time.” She also received an Olivier nomination for “Turn It Out With Tiler Peck and Friends.” On screen, she choreographed for “John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum” and appeared in Netflix’s “Tiny Pretty Things” and Prime Video’s “Étoile.” She is currently scheduled to dance every performance through March 20.

	The design team includes Tony winners Beowulf Boritt (sets), Ken Billington (lighting), William Ivey Long (costumes) and Kai Harada (sound). Orchestrations are by Doug Besterman and Larry Hochman. Sam Davis handles music supervision and dance arrangements, and Jill Green Casting handles casting.

	Anita Waxman is lead producer, with Jana Shea, Patricia R. Klausner/Sharon A. Carr, Emily Blavatnik and Danny Cohen. Iwan Lewis is U.K. executive producer, and Short Street Productions is general manager.

	“We’ve always had big ambitions for this beautiful show, and London is just the beginning,” Waxman said. “We can’t wait to take ‘Little Dancer’ to the world.”

title: Indonesian Director Ariani Darmawan Ends 15-Year Hiatus With ‘Jani Be Good,’ Debuts Trailer Ahead of Tokyo World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indonesian director Ariani Darmawan is ending a 15-year absence from filmmaking with her debut feature, “Jani Be Good,” which will world premiere in
body:
Indonesian director Ariani Darmawan is ending a 15-year absence from filmmaking with her debut feature, “Jani Be Good,” which will world premiere in the Asian Future competition at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival. 

	Variety is debuting the film’s first trailer.

	The drama is titled “Desember Jani” in Indonesian and produced by Jakarta outfit Palari Films. 


	The story takes place over four days in December and tracks four women spanning three generations. At its center is 13-year-old Jani, the youngest in the household. She slowly comes to grasp the different parts the women around her play, while working out how to speak for herself.
	

	Chempa Puteri plays Jani, with Sigi Wimala as Winnie, Hyori Mika as Julia and Tutie Kirana as the grandmother, Oma.

	Darmawan wanted Cyntha Hariadi to write the screenplay from the outset, having read the writer’s short story collection “Manifesto Flora.” “Jani Be Good” is Hariadi’s first feature script.

	“When I started thinking about this film, I was imagining the small things that happen inside a home: the conversations, the tension, and the feelings that often go unspoken. We then developed this story together over three years. Becoming a mother also changed the way I see the relationship between children and parents. From there, Jani grew into my way of looking at these four women characters from different generations, all still learning to understand one another,” said Darmawan.

	The women on the film’s core creative team also span several generations.

	Darmawan was a prominent figure in Indonesian short filmmaking through the late 2000s and early 2010s, and her 2008 short “Sugiharti Halim” was selected for competition at the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival.
	

	“When I invited Ariani to make a film again three years ago, our conversation didn’t start with genre or what kind of film she wanted to make. I asked her what the most extraordinary experience in her life had been while she wasn’t making films. Her answer was becoming a mother. ‘Jani Be Good’ began from that simple conversation. For us at Palari Films, this film isn’t just about a filmmaker’s return after 15 years. It’s about giving space for the voices and experiences of women from different generations to meet in one film,” said producer Meiske Taurisia of Palari Films.

	The project was presented at the Hong Kong Asia Film Financing Forum (HAF) in March this year, ahead of its Tokyo selection. After the festival, “Jani Be Good” will open in Indonesian cinemas on Dec. 10.

	Palari Films, founded in 2016, is led by Taurisia and Muhammad Zaidy. The banner’s “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash” won the Golden Leopard at the 74th Locarno Film Festival. Its other credits include “Aruna and Her Palate,” “Posesif,” “Ali & Ratu Ratu Queens,” “Dear David,” the Netflix original “Borderless Fog” and this year’s “Sleep No More.”

title: Garin Nugroho, Mishima Yukiko, Qiu Jiongjiong Titles Among 15 in Tokyo Film Festival Competition
description: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival has unveiled its complete program, led by a 15-film main competition featuring work by Indonesian directo
body:
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival has unveiled its complete program, led by a 15-film main competition featuring work by Indonesian director Garin Nugroho, Japanese filmmaker Mishima Yukiko and Hong Kong-based Qiu Jiongjiong. 

	The competition spans world and Asian premieres. Seven titles receive world premieres: “The Canary’s Lullaby,” a Taiwan-Japan co-production directed by Ikeda Akira; Qiu Jiongjiong’s “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” produced across Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar; Yamamoto Akira’s Japanese drama “The Intertwining”; Wang Jiangyong’s France-Hong Kong co-production “The Night That Binds Us”; Nugroho’s “Red Before Dawn” from Indonesia; Milcho Manchevski’s North Macedonia-led ensemble “Sister Brother Manhole Cover”; and Mishima Yukiko’s “Two Cigarettes, Three Nights” from Japan.
	

	The remaining eight competition titles arrive as Asian premieres. Lisandro Alonso’s Chile-Argentina co-production “Double Freedom” will screen alongside Teodora Ana Mihai’s Belgian soccer-disaster drama “Heysel 85,” Rubaiyat Hossain’s France-Bangladesh co-production “The Difficult Bride,” Samuele Rossi’s Italian film “Even If Hell Came,” Sun Xun’s Singapore title “Magic Atlas,” Sérgio Graciano’s Portuguese drama “Memories of Prison,” Iranian-Turkish director Bahman Ghobadi’s Turkey-set “Trees Are Watching” and Jelena Maksimović’s Serbian co-production “Until the Day Ends.”


	The Asian Future competitive section will present 10 titles, eight of which receive world premieres. They include Navid Mohammadzadeh’s Iranian film “I’m Nothing Special Really”; Ariani Darmawan’s Indonesian title “Jani Be Good”; Cai Ronglin’s “Miracle Summer” from Japan; South Korean film “On the Heights” by Kim Hyun-min; Tamil Nadu filmmaker Chezhiyan’s Indian entry “The Paper Flower”; Kujiraoka Hironori’s Japanese film “Saravah”; Azamat Shargyn’s Kazakh film “Shyrmauyq”; and Soheil Karimi’s Iranian drama “Silver.” Katski Flores’s Filipino title “EDJOP” and Tareq Daoud’s Switzerland-Turkey co-production “Serife Tavsan” will receive international premieres.
	

	As previously announced, the Gala selection features Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” as the opening film, while Yeon Sang-ho’s “Colony” from South Korea takes the closing slot in a Japanese premiere. Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” serves as the centerpiece. Other Gala titles include Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” Wayne Wang’s “Diary of a Mad Old Man,” Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s “The Beloved” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.”

	The Nippon Cinema Now section will spotlight nine Japanese films. World premieres include Matsumura Shingo’s “Between Us,” Matsubayashi Yoju’s “Okinawa Saudade,” Saito Kisin’s “Kefi,” Ueda Shinichiro’s “Earthlings in Love,” Inudo Isshin’s “Yamazaki Riverside -Over an Actor’s Shoulder-” and “Plastic Love!,” co-directed by Sybilla Patrizia and Clementine Nuttall.

	The World Focus section features titles by Valeska Grisebach, Lav Diaz, Angela Schanelec and Indonesian director Edwin, plus a Taiwan Cinema Renaissance 2026 strand, an Australia Spotlight, a Youssef Chahine centenary retrospective and a tribute program for German filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger.

	The Classics section will present 4K digitally remastered versions of Naruse Mikio’s “When a Woman Ascends the Stairs” and “Scattered Clouds,” alongside a Nikkatsu Roman Porno 55th anniversary retrospective and a TIFF/National Film Archive of Japan retrospective of Mizoguchi Kenji’s work. Additional sections include Women’s Empowerment, Animation — which features a “Women Directors: Diverse Visions” strand — Crosscut Asia+ and Youth.

	Programming director Ichiyama Shozo leads the selection alongside senior programmer Ishizaka Kenji, who oversees Asian Future.

	The festival will run Oct. 26–Nov. 4 in Tokyo.

title: Banijay Entertainment’s Scripted Secret: Find the Talent, Then Back the Ideas
description: With 170 labels across 25 territories, Banijay Entertainment has plenty of scale. But at Iberseries & Platino Industria, Steve Matthews, head of scr
body:
With 170 labels across 25 territories, Banijay Entertainment has plenty of scale. But at Iberseries & Platino Industria, Steve Matthews, head of scripted, creative, made clear that the company’s global strategy doesn’t begin with scale, platforms or market trends. It begins with writers.

	“Good writers, I mean, it really boils down to that,” said Maria Grazia Vairo, director of content at Italy’s Groenlandia, when asked how producers balance commercial appeal with creative ambition.
	

	Matthews concurred, arguing that Banijay’s challenge is to build an international network without flattening the creative identities of its individual companies.


	“I built this large group of companies and then encouraged this granular process where the company has maintained their different creative identities,” he said. “All of these are based on creativity, based on talent, based on writing.” 

	In an interview with Variety, Matthews expanded on the twice-yearly four-day boot camp where Banijay invites writers and producers from the different labels to develop ideas or scripts during that period. “My real pleasure is looking for writers who are episodic writers and are ready to create a show,” he said, noting that the need for training and upskilling new writers and new producers has grown as the streamer boom saw certain development schools in Europe decline.

	The panel brought together Vairo, Simone Oliviera of Brazil’s A Fábrica and Carolina Bang, CEO of Spain’s Pokeepsie Films — three producers working in very different markets but facing the same fundamental challenge: finding material and talent strong enough to cut through an increasingly crowded scripted landscape.
	



	

	



	At Groenlandia, Vairo said the company’s slate has been built around original stories, often drawn from true events and overlooked characters. Its series about Italian pop band 883, for example, was initially conceived as a one-season project before becoming a returning hit.

	“What they’re really looking for are original stories,” Vairo said of the streamers.

	The company’s answer to the quality-versus-commerciality equation is straightforward: writers. Groenlandia has cultivated a reputation as a talent-friendly producer, giving writers creative partners who understand and develop their ideas.

	That relationship, Vairo suggested, is increasingly important as commissioners look for projects that can stand apart rather than simply fit a familiar genre.

	A Fábrica’s Oliveira likewise emphasized the importance of building long-term relationships with creators. The Brazilian company works across premium series, films and sitcoms and is developing several projects with writer Raphael Montes, including adaptations and original series.

	The strategy is less about predicting the next international hit than creating the conditions for one to emerge.

	Pokeepsie’s Bang offered a particularly clear example. The company, known for horror and comedy, moved into young-adult storytelling after Bang discovered the books younger members of her family were reading. She fell for the material and spent years trying to get the project made.

	“We do whatever we like,” Bang said. “If you have in mind to have a success, you will not have it. You have to believe in what you are doing.”

	That instinct is increasingly important in a market where trends can become obsolete before a project reaches production. Matthews cautioned against treating market intelligence as a recipe for development.

	“You never set out to make a commercial show,” he said. “You come into the office and say, ‘Guys, let’s make a commercial show.’ It won’t be good. And therefore, it won’t be commercial either.”

	The trick, he added, is finding the right balance between understanding the market and protecting the creative idea that made the project worth pursuing in the first place.

	“If you robotically go to a panel where one of the guys says, ‘We’re looking for thrillers,’ and then run back to the office and try and develop it, it can be changed by the time you get through it,” Matthews said. “The trick is getting that creative integrity in the thing that you’re trying to make.”
	

	That philosophy also shapes Banijay’s approach to risk. Vairo noted that producing is inherently risky: even strong material can stumble because of casting, financing, commissioning or any number of variables.

	For Matthews, Banijay’s scale can help absorb some of that risk while allowing individual labels to remain relatively nimble.

	“These guys are taking these creative decisions all day, every day,” he said. “The philosophy of getting that balance [is that] these guys can stay small, wind behind them, to come up with something big.”

	The cross-border model is designed less as a factory for uniform content than as a way of connecting creative talent. Matthews described his role as providing support — funding, introductions, development time or access to colleagues in other territories — while allowing producers to lead creatively.

	That becomes particularly relevant as the scripted business contracts and commissioning becomes more selective. Matthews acknowledged that “there’s a lot less work to go around,” but argued that the squeeze could ultimately raise the bar.

	“I genuinely believe that good shows will get made,” he said. “Shows that are manufactured to be commercial will not.”

title: Venice Golden Lion Winner Milcho Manchevski’s ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’ Heads to Tokyo for World Premiere, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” the new feature from Venice Golden Lion winner Milcho Manchevski, will world premiere in the Tokyo International Fil
body:
“Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” the new feature from Venice Golden Lion winner Milcho Manchevski, will world premiere in the Tokyo International Film Festival‘s main competition. 

	Variety is debuting the trailer. 

	Francesca Breccia’s Coccinelle Film Sales is handling the film and will start selling it to international buyers during Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market.


	Manchevski wrote and directed the dark comedy, which centers on Malina and Viktor, a sister and brother getting by hand to mouth at the edges of Macedonian society. To keep going, the pair pilfer bronze busts and manhole covers, and they do it with plenty of attitude. Their chaotic path eventually brings them to a wealthy elderly woman who is blind. Her mix of hardness and kindness pushes them to examine their own sense of right and wrong, and what it means to be devoted to someone.
	

	“Our anti-heroes defiantly refuse to identify as victims,” Manchevski said.

	Sara Klimoska and Filip Trajkovikj lead the cast, with Sonja Mihajlova also on board. Jane Kortoshev is the producer.

	“I was interested in telling a story of great love and unconditional acceptance that is not erotic,” Manchevski said.

	The filmmaker first drew international attention with “Before the Rain,” which took the Golden Lion at Venice along with the Fipresci Prize and went on to earn an Academy Award nomination for best foreign-language film. His later features include “Dust,” the opening-night film at Venice, as well as “Mothers” and “Willow.”

	The new film brings Manchevski back to Tokyo. His last feature, “Kaymak,” also bowed in the festival’s competition as a world premiere.

title: After ‘I Swear’ Scores 7 BAFTA Scotland Nods, Tourette’s Campaigner John Davidson to Watch Ceremony From ‘Separate’ Area Within Venue Following N-Word Controversy
description: Just over than seven months after the British Academy faced one of its biggest controversies in years after the N-word was shouted out during the BA
body:
Just over than seven months after the British Academy faced one of its biggest controversies in years after the N-word was shouted out during the BAFTA Film awards ceremony, BAFTA has had to revisit the moment as it contends with the upcoming BAFTA Scotland awards. 

	The incident — which came to significantly overshadow the 2026 awards ceremony on Feb. 22 — saw John Davidson, the Tourette syndrome activist and inspiration for the film “I Swear,” involuntarily shout the racial slur while Michael B. Jordan and Delroy Lindo were on stage to present the first award of the evening.
	

	“I Swear” has now landed seven BAFTA Scotland nominations, considered the most in the awards’ history. Following the announcement on Thursday, a letter was sent to members from chair Sara Putt and CEO Jane Millichip confirming that major considerations had been undertaken to allow Davidson to attend the upcoming ceremony on Nov. 15 in Glasgow.


	BAFTA said that there had been consultations with organizations such as Tourettes Action and Tourette Scotland and with Davidson. “Following those conversations and our wider risk assessment, we have made adjustments to enable John to attend in the way he has suggested to us, which is to watch the ceremony via video link from a separate relaxed space within the venue together with his family and friends,” it said. 

	An independent review ordered by BAFTA in the wake of the incident concluded that that there were a “number of structural weaknesses in BAFTA’s planning, escalation procedures and crisis coordination arrangements,” but found no evidence of “malicious intent” or “institutional racism.”
	

	The letter to members sent Thursday highlighted this review and said the British Academy had since “worked extensively and consulted widely” to learn from what happened and the “racial harm experienced by our community” and to make its awards as “inclusive and as safe as possible.”

	See the full letter below. 

	As the BAFTA Awards season is now underway, with the Cymru Awards set to take place on Sunday, quickly followed by the Scotland Awards in November, we wanted to take this opportunity to update you on the work BAFTA has undertaken since the Film Awards earlier this year.

	The independent review commissioned by the Board in March identified specific areas for improvement. Since then, the BAFTA team has worked extensively and consulted widely on best practice to learn from what happened in February and the racial harm experienced by our community, and to make our Awards events as inclusive and as safe as possible.

	We have strengthened and centralised our safeguarding, risk assessment and compliance processes, creating a more connected, intersectional and cross-organisational approach to live event planning. We have also simplified communication and escalation routes so concerns can reach the right people quickly, and strengthened briefings for everyone working with us, including hosts, presenters and citation readers.

	With all our guests in mind, we have sought independent advice on inclusion and accessibility best practice from a range of experts. There is no ‘one size fits all’ approach and adjustments should always be tailored, so our planning will aim to better understand individual requirements and consider how this can be supported alongside the safety and dignity of everyone attending. Where adjustments are possible, we will work closely with individuals, supported by experienced access coordinators, to accommodate them.

	We recognise that rebuilding trust requires more than changing processes. The review also challenged us to strengthen BAFTA’s cultural understanding and capability. We have engaged with organisations and experts with experience across race, disability, inclusion and international cultural context and we are developing further training for our staff. This work continues.

	For the upcoming BAFTA Scotland Awards, for which I Swear has received seven nominations, we have worked with both safeguarding and inclusion experts to consider the arrangements necessary to enable John Davidson MBE, whose life inspired I Swear and who is an Executive Producer of the film, to participate in the safest way possible for all.
	

	We have consulted organisations including Tourettes Action and Tourette Scotland and, most importantly, we have been speaking directly to John. Following those conversations and our wider risk assessment, we have made adjustments to enable John to attend in the way he has suggested to us, which is to watch the ceremony via video link from a separate relaxed space within the venue together with his family and friends.

	John has Tourette Syndrome and experiences coprolalia, a type of vocal tic involving the involuntary expression of socially inappropriate words or phrases. These vocalisations, like all tics, are neurological in origin, occur outside of the individual’s control, and do not reflect a person’s views, beliefs, character or intentions.

	At the same time, we know that involuntary vocal tics involving words relating to race, religion, sexuality or other protected characteristics can cause distress and harm to others, and it is BAFTA’s responsibility to plan for and mitigate any such impact on our guests.

	We take this very seriously. These changes reflect a broader principle we are embedding in our Awards planning: listening to people about their needs, preparing carefully, and creating an environment in which everyone is treated with dignity and respect.

	We know that no live event can be entirely risk-free. We will continue to test our processes, review how they operate in practice and be accountable for improving them. We will do everything we can to make sure every guest feels safe, welcome, and included at our Awards.

	Thank you to the members, committees, advisers, community organisations and external experts who have challenged us, shared their experience and helped us improve.

	With best wishes

	Sara and Jane

title: Anne Hathaway Would Rather Have Another Knicks Championship Over a Second Oscar
description:

	Let’s revisit: On April 20, the Knicks lost Game 2 of their NBA Play
body:
When it comes to the New York Knicks, Anne Hathaway is their good luck charm.

	Let’s revisit: On April 20, the Knicks lost Game 2 of their NBA Playoffs series to the Atlanta Hawks. On May 1, Hathaway’s “The Devil Wears Prada 2” premiered and featured a scene where Hathaway’s character chats up Knicks star Karl-Anthony Towns at a Hamptons soiree. The Knicks subsequently went on a historic 13-game winning streak and did not lose again until Game 3 of the NBA Finals on June 9 (Trump attended). Hathaway, a New York City native and lifelong Knicks fan, was jokingly credited for their change in fortune by yours truly and a host of others.
	

	And so, on Wednesday night, Hathaway visited “The Tonight Show” to promote her new erotic thriller “Verity” and host Jimmy Fallon brought up the Knicks meme before gifting “The Odyssey” star, who is five months pregnant, a signed jersey from Knicks savior OG Anunoby. (Hathaway professed her Anunoby fandom after he nearly crashed into her and her son while going into the stands for a ball during a November 2024 game.)


	“Are you serious? Oh my god!” exclaimed Hathaway, before putting the jersey on. The Knicks also sent Hathaway a basket of gifts for her baby, replete with a card reading “All my best” signed by Anunoby. “I’m so excited about my jersey,” she said, playing with it instead of answering Fallon’s questions.

	Later on in the show, Fallon tortured the pregnant Hathaway with a sadistic game called “Best Thing Ever,” forcing her to choose between two cherished things. At one point, he asked her to choose whether she’d rather win another Oscar — she’s a best supporting actress frontrunner for her fiery turn in “The Odyssey” — or have the Knicks win another championship.
	

	“I… I… OK….,” stumbled Hathaway, before choosing another Knicks title.

	“I’m actually, like, the way my nervous system is reacting to that choice is really intense,” she explained.

title: Florence Pugh and Hoon Lee Form the Beating Heart of Netflix’s Rich ‘East of Eden’ Adaptation: TV Review
description: “East of Eden,” the John Steinbeck novel, opens with a place: the author’s native Salinas Valley, the fertile terrain transitioning from the nation’
body:
“East of Eden,” the John Steinbeck novel, opens with a place: the author’s native Salinas Valley, the fertile terrain transitioning from the nation’s frontier to its bread basket at the turn of the 20th century. “East of Eden,” the Netflix limited series created by actor and screenwriter Zoe Kazan, opens with a person: Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), the Eve and Satanic temptress of Steinbeck’s explicit Biblical allegory. “I believe there are monsters born to human parents,” Cathy intones — transplanting Steinbeck’s introduction of his most iconic villain into the mouth of the woman it describes.
	

	This rearrangement doubles as a statement of purpose. Kazan’s adaptation of the literary classic, overseen in partnership with co-showrunner Jeb Stuart (writer of “Die Hard” and “The Fugitive”), is faithful — arguably even more so than the 1955 film directed by her grandfather Elia, previously the book’s best-known screen version. (The feature zeroes in on the final phase of a multigenerational epic, while this series takes on the whole thing.) But emphases and points of view are rearranged to elevate two characters in particular: Cathy, as indicated by the show’s marketing and advance press, and Lee (Hoon Lee), the Chinese American cook whose added dimensions emerge more gradually. These dual portraits aren’t consistently or equally successful, but combined with a lush production and a stellar cast, they’re a case for bringing Steinbeck’s enduring tale of free will, original sin and cyclical tragedy into the 21st century.


	Pugh was an Oscar nominee by her late 20s for her performance in another high-profile adaptation, Greta Gerwig’s “Little Women.” She’s nonetheless spent the last few years without a role quite deserving of her talents. (Getting beamed up into the Marvel machine will do that to a young actor.) Though largely a film star, Pugh had previously done some of her finest work on television, in Korean auteur Park Chan-Wook’s 2018 take on John Le Carré’s “The Little Drummer Girl.” Watching “East of Eden,” which Pugh also executive produced, it’s apparent what called her back to the small screen: In Cathy, she gets a character who’s constantly calculating as her position shifts over decades, from vulnerable girl to reluctant wife to skilled prostitute to grizzled madam. And making hidden depths legible on the surface is some of what Pugh does best.
	

	A teenage Cathy arrives, beaten and bloody, on the Connecticut doorstep of half-brothers Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles Trask (Mike Faist), whose own psychodrama is already well under way. Pit against one another by their father Cyrus (Tracy Letts), a Civil War veteran obsessed with molding his sons into a soldier (Adam) and a farmer (Charles) despite either boy’s natural instincts, the Trasks are already in possession of the emotional inheritance they’ll soon pass on to the next generation. But we see them first through Cathy’s eyes, which burn with an animal intelligence even through a mosaic of bruises and scabs. Adam, simple and trusting, is an easy mark for a desperate woman looking for a life raft. Charles, canny and discerning, is a threat — and maybe a kindred spirit.

	Pugh is fantastic in these early episodes, which establish Cathy as a kind of psychopath in the clinical sense — a creature of instinct who sees any threat to her agency, from parental discipline to full-blown abuse, as a lethal attack to be repaid with interest. Watching her operate is akin to Scarlett Johansson’s performance as a man-eating alien in the 2013 film “Under the Skin”: Cathy operates less out of malice than an innate, unchangeable essence. When she likens her marriage to something that “can be slipped out of, like a poorly made knot,” we understand how inimical she is to any kind of constraint, legal or otherwise. That her means of exit is abandoning her newborn twins is less than sympathetic, but in a different era Cathy would have options beyond a domesticity that never suited her in the first place.

	As the series continues, however, Kazan plays up the explanatory power of an incident from Cathy’s childhood. If Steinbeck believes monsters are born, Kazan seems to be of the school that they’re made. The origin story helps contextualize the misery and self-isolation of Cathy’s later years, as the madam of a Salinas whorehouse. But it also abates the singular ferocity of her early characterization, and concedes to the viewer’s need to find humanity in her. You don’t need to like, or even find a neat cause-and-effect, for Cathy to marvel at her claiming agency at any cost.

	Kazan has said she originally intended for “East of Eden” to run for eight episodes, and there’s some palpable compression in the seven ultimately produced. (Another cost-cutting measure moved the production to New Zealand. While it’s sad to miss out on authentic California landscapes in a story so rooted in geography, cinematographer Stuart Dryburgh gets some stunning, sun-dappled vistas out of the islands’ rolling hills.) “Challengers” star Faist is a surprisingly minimal presence once newlyweds Adam and Cathy set out for Northern California; even before, we don’t get to know Charles well enough for his theory that “kind recognizes kind” in Cathy to resonate. Nor do we get much time with the teenage versions of the couple’s sons Cal (Joseph Zada) and Aaron (Joe Anders) to deepen them beyond vessels for their ancestors’ baggage.
	

	But it’s also clear what Kazan wanted to make space for. Cathy’s ingratiation with, and eventual usurpation of, brothel owner Faye (Martha Plimpton) gets an entire episode. So does an extended interlude with Lee co-written by novelist Alexander Chee, the only installment on which Kazan does not have sole script credit. As in the novel, Lee is an educated and empathetic soul who observes society from its margins. Born in America to railroad workers, Lee speaks in a thickly accented pidgin around racist strangers who expect it of him. Behind closed doors, though, he debates philosophy with neighbor Samuel Hamilton (Ciarán Hinds, so warm you wouldn’t know his role is downsized from the text) and studies the Bible. This pursuit makes Lee the voice of the story’s central theme: timshel, a Hebrew word from the legend of Cain and Abel (or Charles and Adam, or Caleb and Aaron) that translates to “thou mayest” — not “thou shalt,” emphasizing individual choice over unalterable fate.

	In keeping with the concept, this Lee gets more of his own arc, driven by his own decisions and developed enough to rival his employers for the center of the show. There are more details about his parents, a sojourn into San Francisco’s bustling Chinatown and an assertion of autonomy within the Trask household, of which Lee is an essential part. The gender dynamics of Adam and Lee’s arrangement in the season’s latter half are fascinating: as cook, gardener, bookkeeper and active parent, Lee is functionally the twins’ surrogate mother, a fact “East of Eden” never states outright but instead subtly insists on. Hoon Lee is not as famous as Pugh, nor does his character burn as brightly as Cathy’s hatred for societal norms. Yet his calm, quietly wounded demeanor is just as essential to the show, and the way Lee grows more complex over time offsets the way Cathy is somewhat simplified.

	Were “East of Eden” merely a sumptuous period piece, it would still be event viewing, the kind of somber-toned release that announces the onset of Fall TV. Directors Garth Davis (“Lion”) and Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre (“The Mustang”) join a crew of artisans, including production designer Grant Major, costume designer Kirsty Cameron and score composer Laura Karpman, in conjuring a moment in time as specific as the Genesis story is universal. By the episodes’ end, I wasn’t totally convinced a narrative so dependent on the passage of time was an organic fit for the screen. (Pugh gets aged up with cosmetics, but Abbott looks as boyish as ever while Adam attempts to act as patriarch.) Still, the endeavor feels worth it for Pugh and Lee’s standout efforts, which etch their characters deep into one’s memory. Even great books can acquire dust on the shelf; an infusion of feeling helps keep them alive.
	

	All seven episodes of “East of Eden” are now streaming on Netflix.

title: Grup Mediapro Companies Bet on Big Ideas, Local Voices and Cross Border Muscle

body:
Spain’s independent production scene is leaning into a familiar playbook — strong creators, distinctive local stories and plenty of hustle — while looking for new ways to make those stories travel.

	At the 6th Iberseries & Platino Industria confab in Madrid, executives from Imagina (Imagina becomes the new corporate name of Grup Mediapro from Jan. 1, 2027) companies Globomedia, 100 Balas, Big Bang Media, Cimarrón Cine and El Terrat laid out strategies that, despite their different slates, share a common thread: don’t chase scale for scale’s sake. Build projects around talent, stay nimble and find the right production model for each story.
	

	Globomedia’s entertainment slate remains closely tied to comedy, a genre that director general Maria Jose Rodríguez said is embedded in the company’s DNA. The company has been behind influential Spanish TV titles including “Sé lo que hicisteis” and “Caiga quien caiga” — shows that, she argued, helped reshape the country’s television landscape.


	“Comedy is the best tool we have to entertain, generate critical thinking and connect with one another,” Rodríguez said.

	For 100 Balas, real-life stories and creator-driven fiction are at the heart of the strategy. Director General Alejandro Flórez described the company as “a production company with stories, with origins and with authors,” pointing to real cases, investigations and creators capable of building their own worlds.

	The producer is behind scripted thriller “Death in Llanes,” based on the murder of Spanish politician Javier Ardines, and documentary series “Expediente Linares,” about the alleged paranormal phenomena surrounding Madrid’s Palacio de Linares. On the fiction side, titles including “Celeste,” “Su Majestad” and “Yakarta” reflect the company’s focus on projects with strong creative identities.
	

	“At a time when the audiovisual offering is broader than ever, the real differentiator continues to be the stories and those capable of telling them in a unique way,” Flórez said. “It’s not about producing more content. It’s about producing content that leaves a mark.”

	The company is also betting on the second season of “Celeste,” created by Diego San José and starring the ever-popular Carmen Machi, who was honored with the prestigious National Film Prize at San Sebastian Festival, as a tax inspector who delves again into tax evasions, money and powerful interests.

	On international expansion, Flórez said: “We don’t make series thinking about traveling,” he said. “You shouldn’t be afraid of being local.” For Flórez, a distinctly Spanish voice can be precisely what gives a series international legs.

	At Big Bang Media, meanwhile, live television remains a major part of the DNA. General manager Carmen González pointed to “Malas Lenguas,” which has evolved across RTVE’s La 2 and La 1, different time slots and different presenting teams.

	“It’s a typical example in television,” González said of the show’s ability to move between channels and audiences while retaining its identity.

	The producer is also pushing deeper into fiction. “Ser o no ser,” made for RTVE Play, ran for two seasons and targeted younger audiences, while “Pérdida” has expanded internationally via Atresplayer. Big Bang is now developing projects with bestselling author María Dueñas and “La Dama de la Cartuja,” a period drama based on Inma Aguilera’s novel.

	“We’re looking for creators who have a lot to say, as well as literary titles that we believe can make an important leap to the screen,” González said.

	Across the Atlantic-facing Spanish-language market, Cimarrón Cine is taking the borderless approach a step further. CEO-co-founder Santiago López likened the company to Uruguay’s cimarrón dogs, a breed shaped by generations of mixing and adaptation.

	“Cimarrón is also a mixture,” López said. “We started as a mix of two countries and are now a mix of five countries, of very different formats and projects, but above all of very different people.”

	That mix is increasingly feeding original development. López said that five years ago, roughly one in five projects was created in-house; today it is one in three, with the company aiming for one in two.
	

	Its model is deliberately cross-border. Cimarrón has taken Spanish format “El Conquistador del Fin del Mundo” to Mexico and the U.S., shot it in the Dominican Republic and completed work in the Southern Cone. It has also adapted Argentine novel “Cometierra” across Mexico and Uruguay.

	“There is no territory that thinks while the others simply execute,” López said. “We try not to make the stories smaller. We make the project possible so that the story can be possible.”

	Creative director Andrés Gelós summed up the philosophy in more colorful terms: after spending decades as a “lone wolf,” he now sees Cimarrón as a creative “pack.”

	Finally, El Terrat is using almost four decades of comedy and entertainment experience to make a bigger fiction play. General manager Agustín Esteve acknowledged that the company remains best known for entertainment but said its ambition is clear: “Our goal for some time now has been to also be recognized for fiction.”

	Its latest feature, “5 minutos más,” produced with Ikiru for Movistar Plus, premiered at San Sebastián, where Javier Cámara won the Silver Shell for supporting actor. The Berto Romero-scripted film, directed by Javier Ruiz Caldera, mixes comedy, thriller and apocalyptic elements.

	“We struggled for a long time to define what genre this film belongs to,” Esteve said. “But however you define it, it’s a film with a broad audience.”

	El Terrat is also developing Season 2 of “Otro Mundo” for Movistar Plus+ and “Amadas” for 3Cat, while expanding its documentary work with “SerYo,” centered on actor Sergio Peris-Mencheta’s experience during cancer treatment, directed by Marta Solaz, Verónica Díaz Pérez and Peris-Mencheta and the Emmy International-nominated docu ‘Temps Mort,’ co-produced with 3Cat.

	Across all five companies, the message was remarkably consistent: the market may be crowded, budgets may be tight and production increasingly complicated, but distinctive voices still matter.

	For Esteve, the formula comes down to “talent, irreverence, risk, passion, honesty and play” — plus one decidedly unglamorous ingredient: “the desire to work, because without work none of this is possible.”

title: International Oscar Submissions: Cuba, Denmark, Vietnam, Italy, France and More Join the List
